questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: describe what a bacterial cell lacks compared with a eukaryotic cell
questions.stem: A bacterium is drawn with a single circular chromosome, no nuclear envelope, and no membrane-bound organelles. Which description correctly accounts for where its DNA sits?

options.text: In a nucleoid region where the DNA is free in the cytoplasm
Inside a nucleus bounded by a double membrane of its own
options.misconception: gives a bacterium a eukaryotic nucleus

options.text: Inside the chloroplast, where DNA is stored with the pigments
options.misconception: puts bacterial DNA in a chloroplast

options.text: Bound tightly to the inner membrane at one attachment point
options.misconception: claims DNA is tethered to the membrane at a single site

questions.explanation: A bacterium is prokaryotic, so it has no membrane-bound nucleus: its single circular chromosome lies in a nucleoid region of cytoplasm, and the only membrane-bounded structures it may add are specialised ones such as magnetosomes. The tempting belief that a nucleus is compulsory fails because this DNA still works, protected mainly by the cell's own folding proteins rather than an envelope, and a chloroplast is a photosynthetic organelle that bacteria simply do not have.
questions.hint: Ask what the prokaryotic arrangement is called, and where DNA sits without an envelope.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: describe peptidoglycan as sugar chains crosslinked by peptides
questions.stem: A bacterial cell wall is described as a mesh of alternating sugar units joined into long chains, with short peptides bridging one chain to the next. What is this structure called and what holds it together?

options.text: Peptidoglycan, held by peptide crosslinks between the sugar chains
Cellulose, held by hydrogen bonds between parallel glucose chains
options.misconception: confuses the bacterial wall with a plant cell wall

options.text: A lipid bilayer, held by hydrophobic forces between fatty acid tails
options.misconception: treats the cell wall as a membrane of lipids

options.text: Chitin, held by covalent links between nitrogen-containing sugars
options.misconception: confuses peptidoglycan with the fungal wall polysaccharide

questions.explanation: The mesh described is peptidoglycan: glycan means sugar, and the long alternating sugar chains are crosslinked by short peptides into a single strong sacculus that resists bursting. The tempting belief that this is cellulose fails because cellulose is a plant wall polymer joined by glycosidic bonds between sugars, with no peptide crosslinks, and treating the wall as a lipid bilayer confuses a structural polymer with the cell membrane underneath it.
questions.hint: The name splits into sugar and peptide; use both halves.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: relate bacterial ribosome size to the selectivity of protein synthesis inhibitors
questions.stem: A bacterium is described as having 70S ribosomes made of 30S and 50S subunits, while human cytoplasm has 80S ribosomes made of 40S and 60S subunits. Why does that difference matter for treatment?

options.text: Drugs built for 70S ribosomes hit bacterial protein synthesis, not ours
The 70S size lets a bacterium build proteins much faster than we can
options.misconception: claims ribosome size sets the overall rate of synthesis

options.text: 70S ribosomes are larger, so bacteria need more of them per cell
options.misconception: mislabels S values as physical size to force a contradiction

options.text: The difference stops human cells from making any protein at all
options.misconception: thinks a ribosome mismatch blocks all human protein synthesis

questions.explanation: The S values describe sedimentation rate, and the two ribosome types differ enough in shape and rRNA sequence that drugs designed to fit the 70S bacterial large subunit block bacterial translation while sparing the 80S human version, which is the basis of selective toxicity. The tempting belief that a bigger sedimentation value means a faster or larger ribosome fails because Svedberg units are not additive and describe how fast a particle settles, not how fast protein is made.
questions.hint: Ask which ribosome the drug's shape is a poor fit for.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: state the functions of a bacterial capsule
questions.stem: A species of Streptococcus is described as being surrounded by a loose, well-organised layer of polysaccharide lying outside the cell wall. What does that layer let the bacterium do?

options.text: Adhere to surfaces and resist phagocytosis and drying out
Build peptidoglycan, since the capsule supplies the crosslinking peptides
options.misconception: assigns wall-building to the capsule instead of the wall

options.text: Store glycogen, because polysaccharide layers are the storage form
options.misconception: treats an external layer as a carbohydrate store

options.text: Carry out aerobic respiration, since oxygen enters through the capsule
options.misconception: makes the capsule a respiratory organelle

questions.explanation: A capsule is a protective and adhesive layer: its polysaccharide keeps the cell from drying out, helps it stick to host tissues and to other cells in a biofilm, and makes it slippery enough to escape phagocytosis. The tempting belief that the capsule builds the wall confuses two adjacent structures, because the peptide crosslinks that assemble peptidoglycan sit in the wall itself, under the capsule, not in the slime layer above it.
questions.hint: Ask what a layer outside the cell wall would physically do first.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: list the structural components of a virus particle
questions.stem: An electron micrograph is described as showing a particle with a protein coat of repeating subunits surrounding a genome, and a fatty envelope with embedded proteins in some particles. Which parts of a virus do these correspond to?

options.text: A capsid of capsomeres, the genome inside it, and an envelope
A cell wall of peptidoglycan, the genome, and a plasma membrane
options.misconception: reads a viral envelope as a peptidoglycan cell wall

options.text: A ribosome cluster, the genome, and a mitochondrion for energy
options.misconception: gives a virus ribosomes and a mitochondrion

options.text: A flagellum, the genome, and a chloroplast for photosynthesis
options.misconception: gives a virus photosynthetic organelles

questions.explanation: The repeating protein subunits make up the capsid, whose protein shell is called a capsomere, and it encloses either DNA or RNA as the genome; many viruses also carry a lipoprotein envelope studded with proteins they borrowed from a host membrane. The tempting belief that the coat is a cell wall fails because viruses have no cytoplasm, no peptidoglycan and no metabolism, and there is no ribosome or organelle in the particle at all.
questions.hint: Name the protein shell built from repeating subunits.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: state what a plasmid is and what it can carry
questions.stem: A bacterial cell is described as carrying a small circular piece of DNA of about 3000 base pairs that is separate from its single chromosome. What is this molecule, and why does it matter?

options.text: A plasmid, which can carry accessory genes such as antibiotic resistance
A second chromosome, which doubles the DNA available for replication
options.misconception: treats a plasmid as a second full chromosome

options.text: A fragment of degraded messenger RNA left over from last week
options.misconception: confuses a DNA replicon with degraded messenger RNA

options.text: A fragment of the cell wall picked up and stored by the membrane
options.misconception: gives a plasmid a structural rather than genetic role

questions.explanation: A plasmid is a small independently replicating circle of DNA kept apart from the chromosome, and it commonly carries accessory genes: antibiotic resistance, virulence factors, or the genes for degrading unusual carbon sources. The tempting belief that it is a second chromosome fails because a plasmid is orders of magnitude smaller and carries only a handful of genes, and because it can be gained or lost without the cell losing viability, which is exactly why resistance plasmids spread so easily.
questions.hint: Ask whether the copy carries the cell's basic housekeeping instructions.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain the Gram stain outcome from wall thickness and retention
questions.stem: A figure shows two micrographs of the same species treated by a Gram stain. In the first the cells are uniformly dark purple and rounded, and in the second the cells are pink and rod-shaped. What accounts for the difference in colour?

options.text: Peptidoglycan thickness differs, so one wall retains the purple stain
One species lacks a cell wall, so it takes up the pink counterstain
options.misconception: attributes the stain result to a completely absent wall

options.text: The purple species absorbed more oxygen during the staining step
options.misconception: invents an oxygen-dependent cause for the stain difference

options.text: The pink species grew at a warmer temperature during the incubation
options.misconception: links a Gram result to growth temperature

questions.explanation: The Gram stain separates bacteria on wall thickness. Gram-positive cells have a thick peptidoglycan layer that retains the crystal violet and iodine complex after alcohol decolourisation, so they stay purple, while Gram-negative cells have a thin peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane that the alcohol dissolves, so they lose the purple and take up the pink counterstain. The tempting belief that the pink cells have no wall fails because they do have one; it is simply too thin, and too masked by the outer membrane, to hold the complex.
questions.hint: Think about what the decolouriser does to a thick versus a thin wall.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: match bacterial cell shapes to their names
questions.stem: A figure shows three organisms: one is a perfectly spherical cell, one is a straight cylinder with rounded ends, and one is a short curved comma. Which name belongs to the comma-shaped cell?

options.text: A vibrio, described as a curved comma-shaped bacillus
A coccus, described as a curved comma-shaped bacillus
options.misconception: pairs the name coccus with a curved rod description

options.text: A bacillus, described as a curved comma-shaped coccus
options.misconception: pairs the name bacillus with a spherical description

options.text: A spirillum, described as a rigid straight rod with rounded ends
options.misconception: describes a straight rod under the name for a spiral form

questions.explanation: The suffix describes shape: coccus means spherical, bacillus means rod, and vibrio means a curved comma-shaped rod, which is the organism drawn. The tempting confusion of pairing a name with the wrong shape is easy to fall into because the Latin roots are unfamiliar, but spirillum and spirochete are reserved for longer helical forms, so a single short curve is a vibrio, and a straight cylinder is a bacillus whatever its length.
questions.hint: Match each ending to the shape it names, then pick the curve.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain what an endospore does and what it does not do
questions.stem: Certain bacteria form a thick-coated dormant structure inside the cell, with the cytoplasm dehydrated and the DNA protected by calcium and dipicolinic acid. What does that structure accomplish?

options.text: Survival of heat, desiccation and chemicals, not rapid reproduction
Rapid reproduction, since each spore becomes two new cells
options.misconception: treats spore formation as a reproductive division

options.text: Resistance to antibiotics, since the coat excludes every drug
options.misconception: credits the spore coat with universal drug resistance

options.text: Nitrogen fixation, since the coat converts air into ammonia
options.misconception: gives a survival structure a nitrogen-fixing function

questions.explanation: An endospore is a survival state: the cell dehydrates, concentrates calcium and dipicolinic acid, and builds a multilayered coat so that one cell can survive boiling, drying, radiation or bleach and germinate when conditions improve. The tempting belief that it is a reproductive structure fails because one cell produces one spore, which later yields one cell, so the population does not grow; that is also why spore survival is not the same as antibiotic resistance, since many spore-formers are fully susceptible once they germinate and grow.
questions.hint: Count how many cells come out of one spore.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a flagellum from pili by structure and function
questions.stem: A bacterium is described as having two kinds of surface protein structure: one is a long helical filament driven by a rotary motor, and the other consists of many short straight bristles. Which does what?

options.text: The filament propels the cell; the bristles attach it to surfaces
The filament attaches the cell; the bristles drive it forward
options.misconception: swaps the motor and attachment functions

options.text: Both structures move the cell, one faster than the other
options.misconception: treats pili as a second kind of propeller

options.text: Both structures carry plasmids between neighbouring cells
options.misconception: makes every appendage a conjugation device

questions.explanation: The long helical filament with a rotary motor is the flagellum, which drives swimming by pushing against liquid, while the short straight bristles are pili or fimbriae, shorter, thinner, far more numerous and used for attachment to surfaces, host cells, or each other in a biofilm. The tempting belief that both propel the cell fails because pili cannot generate thrust; only one of the pilus types, the sex pilus, draws cells together, and it does that by retracting, not by swimming.
questions.hint: Ask which structure has a motor and which one has many copies.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify the exponential phase from plotted growth data
questions.stem: A closed broth culture is sampled every hour. The turbidity readings are 0.02, 0.03, 0.09, 0.30, 0.95, 2.9, 8.8, 26, 27, 27 and 26 across eleven hours. Which phase accounts for the stretch from 0.30 to 26, and what is happening there?

options.text: Exponential phase, where each cell divides at a fixed interval
Lag phase, where cells are adapting before any division occurs
options.misconception: calls rapid multiplication a period of adaptation

options.text: Stationary phase, where growth and death are exactly balanced
options.misconception: labels a steep rise as a plateau

options.text: Death phase, where nutrients run out and the cells all lyse
options.misconception: labels a rising count as mass lysis

questions.explanation: From 0.30 to 26 the readings roughly triple every hour, which is a constant multiplication factor per unit time, the signature of exponential growth: each cell divides at a fixed interval, and resources are still abundant. The tempting belief that this stretch is the lag phase confuses rate with readiness, because a lag phase produces almost no change in turbidity, and the stationary phase is the flat 27, 27, 26 region where new cells form only as fast as others die.
questions.hint: Look for an interval with a constant multiplication factor.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: calculate a population size from a doubling time
questions.stem: A culture starts with 500 cells of a bacterium that doubles every 20 minutes while in exponential phase. How many cells are present after 3 hours of growth?

options.text: 256,000 cells
1,024 cells
options.misconception: counts doublings from one cell and forgets the starting population

options.text: 128,000 cells
options.misconception: loses one doubling by treating 3 hours as 100 minutes

options.text: 4,500 cells
options.misconception: adds 500 per doubling instead of multiplying by two

questions.explanation: Three hours is 180 minutes, which at 20 minutes per doubling is 9 doublings, and each doubling multiplies by two, so the factor is 2 to the 9, which is 512. Multiplying that by the 500 cells already present gives 256,000 cells. The tempting shortcut of adding 500 each time produces a straight line and only 4,500 cells, which describes linear growth, and starting from one cell gives 512 while ignoring the population the culture was inoculated with.
questions.hint: Divide the total time by the doubling time, then raise two to that power.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: classify bacteria by their oxygen requirement
questions.stem: Three cultures are grown in separate tubes. Species P grows only where oxygen is present, species N grows only where oxygen is absent, and species F grows in either condition, though it grows better with oxygen. What are these three called?

options.text: P is an obligate aerobe, N an obligate anaerobe, F a facultative anaerobe
P is a facultative anaerobe, N an obligate aerobe, F an aerotolerant anaerobe
options.misconception: swaps aerobic and anaerobic labels between the species

options.text: P is an obligate anaerobe, N an obligate aerobe, F a halophile
options.misconception: assigns salt tolerance to a species defined by oxygen use

options.text: P is a saprophyte, N a parasite, and F a free-living species
options.misconception: confuses oxygen requirements with ecological nutrition

questions.explanation: The labels follow from whether oxygen is required, tolerated, or fatal. An obligate aerobe such as Pseudomonas needs oxygen as a terminal electron acceptor, an obligate anaerobe such as Clostridium is poisoned by it, and a facultative anaerobe such as Escherichia coli switches on aerobic respiration when oxygen is present and switches to fermentation when it is not. The tempting belief that aerotolerant means it prefers oxygen fails, because an aerotolerant anaerobe ignores oxygen entirely and still ferments in its presence.
questions.hint: Read the labels as strict requirements, strict exclusions, and optional use.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why a virus can replicate only inside a host cell
questions.stem: A virus grown in cell-free broth stays intact and does not multiply, but it multiplies rapidly once a living host cell is supplied. What does that behaviour show about the virus?

options.text: It has no ribosomes or metabolism of its own, so it needs the cell
It has its own ribosomes, but they work only at thirty-seven degrees
options.misconception: gives the virus ribosomes of its own

options.text: It feeds on sugars in the broth, but only if a cell is present
options.misconception: treats a virus as a cell that feeds heterotrophically

options.text: It divides by binary fission, but needs warmth to start dividing
options.misconception: credits a virus with bacterial-style binary fission

questions.explanation: A virus particle contains a genome and proteins but no ribosomes, no enzymes for energy production and no metabolism of its own, so it can only redirect a host cell's ribosomes, nucleotides and ATP to assemble new virions. The tempting belief that it has its own ribosomes fails because the particle as described holds no translation machinery at all, and describing it as feeding or dividing by binary fission borrows the vocabulary of cells, which viruses are not.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the particle would have to be borrowed for assembly.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify the three main bacterial targets of antibiotics
questions.stem: A clinician lists amoxicillin, erythromycin and rifampin as antibacterial drugs. What shared property lets these drugs work, and which bacterial processes do they hit?

options.text: They target structures bacteria have and cells like ours lack: wall, ribosome, DNA enzyme
They kill any cell dividing quickly, whether bacterial or human
options.misconception: reduces selective toxicity to a division-rate effect

options.text: They dissolve bacterial membranes, which human cells also contain
options.misconception: claims human cells lack membranes too

options.text: They boost the immune system so it clears the infection faster
options.misconception: misclassifies antibacterial drugs as immune stimulators

questions.explanation: Selective toxicity comes from difference: amoxicillin blocks peptidoglycan crosslinking, erythromycin blocks the 70S large ribosomal subunit, and rifampin blocks bacterial RNA polymerase, none of which a human cell has. The tempting belief that these drugs merely kill fast-dividing cells fails because human gut and bone marrow cells also divide quickly, and the human ribosome, DNA polymerases and cell membranes all differ from the bacterial versions, which is where the selectivity actually lies.
questions.hint: Ask what each target has in common across three unrelated drugs.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why penicillin kills only actively growing bacteria
questions.stem: Penicillin is described as binding the transpeptidase enzymes that crosslink peptidoglycan strands, so a growing cell cannot complete its wall. Why does an infected, non-growing culture sometimes survive treatment?

options.text: The drug only harms cells actively building new wall material
The drug is neutralised by any bacteria that make a thick capsule
options.misconception: credits capsules with inactivating penicillin

options.text: The drug is destroyed by the bacterial ribosome during translation
options.misconception: says ribosomes metabolise the antibiotic

options.text: The drug only works when bacteria are in a group, not alone
options.misconception: claims penicillin needs a group of cells to act

questions.explanation: Penicillin blocks a step that only matters while a cell is making new wall, so a bacterium that is not dividing has nothing to crosslink and is unaffected, and a dormant population inside a biofilm therefore survives even when the drug is present. Once such cells resume growth the wall cannot be finished and the cell osmotically lyses, which is why beta-lactams work best against rapidly dividing infections. The tempting belief that capsules destroy the drug fails because the resistance mechanism that does this is the enzyme beta-lactamase, not the capsule.
questions.hint: Ask which step in the cell's schedule the drug interrupts.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain the role of decomposer microbes in nutrient cycling
questions.stem: In a forest, leaves fall and tree trunks die, yet the soil nitrogen and phosphorus levels do not fall to zero. Which group of organisms is chiefly responsible for that recycling?

options.text: Bacteria and fungi, which secrete enzymes and absorb the released nutrients
Herbivorous insects, which eat the dead wood and return the nutrients
options.misconception: gives decomposers the role of a consumer diet

options.text: Photosynthetic plants, which take nutrients from soil as they respire
options.misconception: has plants absorbing nutrients through respiration

options.text: Wind and rain, which physically dissolve the minerals out of the litter
options.misconception: credits abiotic factors with biological mineralisation

questions.explanation: Most of the work is done by decomposer bacteria and fungi, which secrete extracellular enzymes that cut dead organic material into small molecules they can absorb, converting locked carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus into inorganic forms that plants can take up again. The tempting belief that insects or plants do the recycling fails because a consumer only moves nutrients between organisms rather than releasing them from dead matter, and abiotic factors can redistribute minerals but cannot break large polymers into absorbable units.
questions.hint: Ask which organisms secrete enzymes into the dead material itself.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify the bacterial role in converting atmospheric nitrogen to ammonia
questions.stem: Most organisms cannot use the nitrogen gas making up most of the atmosphere, yet crop fields still accumulate usable nitrogen. Which organisms close that gap, and what is the process called?

options.text: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, converting nitrogen gas into ammonia
Nitrifying bacteria, converting ammonia into nitrite and nitrate
options.misconception: confuses nitrogen fixation with nitrification

options.text: Denitrifying bacteria, converting nitrate back into nitrogen gas
options.misconception: confuses nitrogen fixation with denitrification

options.text: Decomposer fungi, converting dead protein into amino acids
options.misconception: credits fixation to decomposition of organic nitrogen

questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, including free-living Azotobacter and symbiotic Rhizobium in legume root nodules, run the energetically expensive step of reducing nitrogen gas to ammonia using the enzyme nitrogenase, and that ammonia is the entry point for all usable nitrogen in the ecosystem. The tempting confusion with nitrification fails because nitrifying bacteria only oxidise ammonia that is already fixed into nitrite and nitrate, and denitrification does the reverse, returning nitrogen to the air.
questions.hint: Find the step that starts from nitrogen gas in the atmosphere.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain enzymatic antibiotic inactivation by beta-lactamase
questions.stem: A resistant isolate grows on amoxicillin agar, and the laboratory detects high levels of an enzyme that opens the drug's strained beta-lactam ring. Why does that enzyme defeat the drug?

options.text: It hydrolyses the ring, so the drug can no longer bind its target
It thickens the cell wall, so the drug cannot reach the membrane
options.misconception: describes a physical barrier instead of drug inactivation

options.text: It pumps the drug out, so less of it ever reaches the enzyme target
options.misconception: describes efflux rather than enzymatic destruction

options.text: It repairs the crosslinks after the drug blocks the transpeptidase
options.misconception: describes target repair rather than drug destruction

questions.explanation: Beta-lactamase hydrolyses the four-membered beta-lactam ring that carries the drug's reactive group, and once that ring is opened the molecule no longer resembles the substrate the transpeptidase accepts, so crosslinking resumes and the cell survives. This is inactivation by destruction of the drug itself, and it is why a resistance gene can protect a cell that has an entirely unchanged target. The tempting belief that a thicker wall is the mechanism fails because wall thickness changes drug susceptibility slowly, not enzymatically in seconds.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the drug molecule, not to the cell.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain how efflux pumps lower intracellular antibiotic concentration
questions.stem: A resistant isolate carries an extra membrane protein described as exporting tetracycline out of the cell using proton motive force, so the internal concentration stays far below the external one. Why is the cell protected?

options.text: The target is never exposed to a high enough drug level to bind it
The exported drug is destroyed by the pump as it leaves the cell
options.misconception: confuses export with enzymatic drug destruction

options.text: The pumped drug cannot re-enter because the membrane pores have closed
options.misconception: invents pore closure as the protection mechanism

options.text: The pump adds extra copies of the target for the drug to bind
options.misconception: claims the pump increases the number of drug targets

questions.explanation: Drugs work by binding their targets, and efflux holds the internal concentration below the level needed to occupy enough of the target, so the ribosome or enzyme carries on working and the cell tolerates a dose that kills a susceptible strain. The pump moves intact drug out using proton motive force, which is why it is an export mechanism rather than a destruction mechanism. The tempting belief that the pumped drug is degraded confuses two different resistance routes, since enzymatic inactivation happens in the fluid and export happens across the membrane.
questions.hint: Link the internal concentration back to whether the target can be occupied.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain how target-site alteration produces resistance
questions.stem: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus resists beta-lactams although it still makes a thick peptidoglycan wall and still carries penicillin-binding proteins. What must have changed in these cells?

options.text: The binding proteins have a reshaped active site that fits the drug poorly
The cell has stopped making peptidoglycan altogether to save material
options.misconception: assumes resistance requires losing the wall entirely

options.text: The wall has thickened so much that no drug can pass through it
options.misconception: reduces target change to a diffusion barrier

options.text: The ribosome has become 80S, so the drugs no longer match the cell
options.misconception: confuses a wall target with ribosomal sedimentation values

questions.explanation: Resistance here is target alteration: the bacterium acquired a mecA gene for a penicillin-binding protein, PBP2a, whose active site no longer accommodates beta-lactams, so crosslinking continues while the drug can no longer inhibit the enzyme. The tempting belief that the wall is gone or simply too thick fails because the wall is essential and fully present, and the mechanism has to be at the level of the drug-enzyme fit, since a diffusion barrier would reduce the dose needed only marginally.
questions.hint: Keep every structure the same and change only the drug's fit.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish biofilm tolerance from heritable resistance
questions.stem: Bacteria growing in a shared polysaccharide matrix on a catheter tolerate a hundred times the antibiotic concentration that kills the same strain in broth. Why is that different from genetic resistance?

options.text: The matrix and slow growth limit penetration, and the cells revert when dispersed
The matrix contains antibiotic-degrading enzymes, so resistance is inherited
options.misconception: claims matrix tolerance is always genetic resistance

options.text: The cells copy faster inside the matrix, outgrowing the drug's effect
options.misconception: asserts faster division inside a biofilm

options.text: The cells acquire plasmid genes inside the matrix within hours
options.misconception: assumes resistance genes appear within a few hours

questions.explanation: Biofilm tolerance is physiological rather than inherited: the polysaccharide matrix binds and slows drug penetration, cells deep inside are slow-growing or dormant and therefore hit by drugs that need active growth, and the persisters survive. Scatter the biofilm and the same strain returns to normal susceptibility, which proves no genetic change was needed. The tempting belief that enzymes in the matrix make this resistance fails because that is genuine enzymatic inactivation, which is a separate mechanism that does survive transfer.
questions.hint: Ask whether the trait persists after the cells are dispersed and regrown.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Antibiotics: Reading a Zone of Inhibition
questions.learningObjective: interpret a zone of inhibition as a measure of susceptibility
questions.stem: Two discs of the same antibiotic are placed on lawns of two strains. Strain A grows right up to the disc edge with no clear ring, while strain B shows a 22 millimetre clear ring around its disc on an otherwise confluent lawn. What does the comparison show?

options.text: B is susceptible, since the drug diffused out and stopped its growth
A is susceptible, since it grew nearest to the highest drug level
options.misconception: reads growth near the disc as drug effectiveness

options.text: Both are resistant, since a clear ring means the disc lost potency
options.misconception: interprets a clear zone as drug breakdown

options.text: B is resistant, since a 22 millimetre ring reflects a thick cell wall
options.misconception: interprets a large zone as a physical barrier

questions.explanation: The antibiotic diffuses outward from the disc and creates a concentration gradient, so a clear ring means growth was inhibited wherever the drug exceeded the strain's threshold, and a 22 millimetre zone on a confluent lawn means strain B is susceptible at that concentration. The tempting belief that strain A is susceptible because it grew closest fails because growth closest to the disc means the drug never stopped it, and the zone is a measurement of inhibition rather than of wall thickness.
questions.hint: Ask what the drug concentration is at the edge of each lawn.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: read a minimum inhibitory concentration from a dilution series
questions.stem: A broth dilution series is prepared with antibiotic concentrations of 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 8 micrograms per millilitre. Turbidity appears in the tubes at 0.5, 1 and 2 micrograms per millilitre, and the tubes at 4 and 8 stay clear. What is the minimum inhibitory concentration?

options.text: 4 micrograms per millilitre
2 micrograms per millilitre
options.misconception: reads the highest turbid tube as the threshold

options.text: 8 micrograms per millilitre
options.misconception: picks the highest concentration tested rather than the lowest effective one

options.text: 0.5 micrograms per millilitre
options.misconception: reports the lowest concentration at which growth was seen

questions.explanation: The minimum inhibitory concentration is the lowest drug concentration that visibly prevents growth, so the search moves down the series from the clear end: growth persists at 2 micrograms per millilitre and is absent at 4, making 4 the MIC. The tempting belief that the answer is the last turbid tube reads the threshold from the wrong side, and the highest concentration tested is irrelevant, since the clinical goal is the least drug that works.
questions.hint: Find the first clear tube reading upward from the growth end.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: describe conjugation as plasmid transfer between cells
questions.stem: A figure shows two rod-shaped bacteria touching end to end through a thin protein tube, with one copy of a small circular plasmid drawn in each cell and an arrow showing the plasmid passing from one cell into the other. What is happening, and what does it explain?

options.text: Conjugation, so a resistance plasmid can jump between cells of one species
Binary fission, so one cell has divided into two new cells
options.misconception: reads a plasmid transfer diagram as cell division

options.text: Transformation, so free plasmid DNA is taken up from the surroundings
options.misconception: confuses cell-to-cell contact with DNA uptake from broth

options.text: Transduction, so a bacteriophage is carrying the plasmid between cells
options.misconception: confuses a sex pilus with a virus vector

questions.explanation: The figure shows conjugation: a donor cell draws a copy of a plasmid to its own surface, establishes a mating bridge through the sex pilus, and transfers the plasmid to a recipient, which then becomes resistant and can pass it on. The tempting confusion with transformation fails because transformation takes up naked DNA released into the environment rather than moving a plasmid through direct contact, and transduction needs a bacteriophage, none of which appears in the drawing.
questions.hint: Notice that the two cells are in direct contact, and no virus is present.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish transformation, transduction and conjugation
questions.stem: Three routes move resistance genes between bacteria. One involves naked DNA taken from the environment, one uses a bacteriophage as the carrier, and one requires direct cell-to-cell contact. Which route is the one needing contact?

options.text: Conjugation, which moves a plasmid through direct cell contact
Transformation, which moves a plasmid through direct cell contact
options.misconception: labels uptake of naked DNA as a contact process

options.text: Transduction, which moves a plasmid through direct cell contact
options.misconception: labels a phage-mediated transfer as a contact process

options.text: None of them, since all three require direct cell contact
options.misconception: insists every transfer route needs physical contact

questions.explanation: Conjugation is the contact-dependent route: a donor transfers plasmid DNA through a mating bridge to a recipient. Transformation needs no donor cell at all, since the cell takes up free DNA shed by lysed bacteria, and transduction needs a bacteriophage that packages host DNA by accident, not contact between two live cells. The tempting belief that all three require contact fails because two of the three can occur in a well-mixed broth with cells kept apart.
questions.hint: Two of the three routes work in a broth with no cells touching.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an error in attributing a viral illness to underdosing
questions.stem: A patient with a confirmed influenza infection is given amoxicillin, improves not at all, and a relative concludes the dose must have been too low. What is the flaw in that reasoning?

options.text: Influenza is caused by a virus, which has no bacterial target for the drug
Amoxicillin is absorbed slowly, so a larger dose would work better
options.misconception: explains viral drug failure by poor absorption

options.text: Influenza bacteria hide inside cells where the drug cannot reach
options.misconception: asserts that influenza is caused by bacteria

options.text: The drug works only by mouth, so the route given was wrong
options.misconception: attaches the failure to an administration route

questions.explanation: Influenza is caused by an influenza virus, and a virus particle has no peptidoglycan, no 70S ribosome and no bacterial DNA polymerase, so there is nothing for amoxicillin to bind and no dose of it will help. The tempting belief that underdosing explains the failure fails because dose only matters when the drug has a target at all, and a dose large enough to matter would instead damage the patient's own gut flora.
questions.hint: Ask what structures the drug needs that a virus particle lacks.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: infer plasmid spread from an outbreak and antibiogram
questions.stem: An intensive care unit records four patients infected by the same methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus strain within one week. All four isolates grow in oxacillin, and plasmid analysis finds an identical 2700 base pair plasmid in every isolate. The unit points to one shared sink as the source. Which conclusion is best supported, and what does it imply?

options.text: One resistance plasmid spread between patients, implying contact spread in the unit
Four unrelated strains mutated separately, implying random chance mutation
options.misconception: attributes a shared plasmid to independent chance mutation

options.text: Every patient was under-dosed, implying a hospital-wide prescribing error
options.misconception: blames under-dosing where the evidence shows transmission

options.text: The organism is now a virus, implying methicillin acted on a viral genome
options.misconception: concludes that resistance means the pathogen changed kingdom

questions.explanation: An identical plasmid in all four isolates is the strongest available evidence, because one copy of the resistance gene spreading horizontally by conjugation explains both the shared resistance and the tight timing, and a contaminated sink or shared equipment is a plausible route for it. The tempting belief that four strains mutated independently fails because independent mutations would not produce identical plasmids, and resistance is a trait acquired by existing bacteria rather than a change in what kind of organism it is.
questions.hint: Compare what independent mutations would predict against an identical plasmid.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a claim that a plateau means bacteria stopped dividing
questions.stem: A culture's optical density rises, then holds flat for six hours, then declines. A student concludes that the bacteria stopped growing only because the nutrient supply was used up. Evaluate that conclusion.

options.text: The plateau means division balanced death, and waste plus crowding also contribute
The plateau proves the bacteria have all died and the culture is now sterile
options.misconception: reads a steady optical density as a dead sterile culture

options.text: The plateau means the bacteria have permanently stopped taking up nutrients
options.misconception: equates a plateau with permanent cessation of nutrient uptake

options.text: The plateau can only follow a temperature rise that killed the dividing cells
options.misconception: invents a temperature rise as the only possible cause

questions.explanation: A flat optical density means cells are still being added at the same rate as they are lost, so growth has not stopped: the approach to that balance comes from nutrients falling, waste accumulating and crowding limiting division, and the later fall shows the loss side finally winning. The tempting belief that a plateau means a dead or sterile culture fails because a dying culture's optical density drops and a sterile one reads as clear, so the plateau itself proves metabolism continues.
questions.hint: Ask what the flat reading says about the balance between division and death.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: justify phage therapy and name what limits it
questions.stem: A bacteriophage can choose a lytic cycle that destroys its host bacterium, or a lysogenic cycle in which its genome stays inside the bacterium and copies passively as the cell divides. Explain why a treatment aimed at clearing a bacterial infection would want the lytic cycle, and name what limits that strategy.

answer.exemplar: Only the lytic cycle destroys the pathogen, because it ends in lysis of the bacterial cell with release of new virions, whereas a lysogenic genome is integrated into the bacterial chromosome, so the phage is carried along inside a bacterium that keeps dividing and keeps growing. A treatment wants killing, so it wants lysis. The limits follow from the same biology: bacteria resist phages by losing or mutating the receptor, by restriction enzymes that cut foreign DNA, and by CRISPR cassettes that store and target phage sequences, and because the treatment spares lysogenic cells, that reservoir can later release phage and reseed the population. The tempting wrong belief is that adding more phage always forces the lytic route, when the decision belongs to the virus's own regulatory switch, driven by the host's physiological condition rather than by the dose given.

questions.explanation: A lytic phage ends its cycle by lysing the host and releasing virions, which removes that bacterium, whereas a lysogenic genome sits in the bacterial chromosome and is copied along with it, so the cell survives, keeps dividing and keeps carrying the phage. That is why clearing an infection requires lysis, and why temperate phages are unreliable tools. The limits are bacterial: receptor loss or mutation, restriction enzymes that cut incoming DNA, and CRISPR cassettes that recognise and destroy matching phage sequences, plus the lysogenic reservoir itself, which the treatment never touches.
questions.hint: Follow what happens to the host cell in each cycle before naming the resistance routes.
